modelo-de-recompensa.d: A network that takes a prompt \(x\) and a response \(y\) and returns a scalar \(r(x,y)\) that summarizes human preferences. It is usually an LLM with its lm_head replaced by a scalar head read at the EOS token, trained on pairs with the loss \(-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l)\).

escala-likert.d: An absolute score on ordered levels (e.g., 1–7, 0–4). Cheap per response and carries magnitude information, but sensitive to each annotator's personal ruler. HelpSteer uses 0–4 on five attributes.

rotulo-suave.d: A label given as a distribution instead of 0/1: a tie becomes (½, ½); an AI labeler might give 0.6/0.4. The loss becomes the cross-entropy against that distribution, and the optimum is \(\Delta^* = \log(\mu_1/\mu_2)\).

coleta-on-policy.d: Collecting new preference pairs from the current policy's responses, in rounds, and retraining the RM on them. It keeps the RM within the distribution the policy produces after RL (Anthropic: weekly cadence; Llama 2: iterative).

concordancia-entre-anotadores.d: How often two annotators give the same judgment on the same item. For LLM preferences it sits between ~63% and ~77%, and it works as the practical ceiling on the accuracy of an RM evaluated against humans.

kappa-de-cohen.d: Agreement between two annotators with chance discounted: \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1-p_e)\), where \(p_o\) is the observed agreement and \(p_e\) the agreement expected from the marginals. It equals 1 for perfect agreement and 0 when there is nothing beyond chance.

kappa-ponderado.d: A version of κ for ordinal scales in which each disagreement weighs \(w_{ij} = (i-j)^2/(k-1)^2\): disagreeing between neighboring levels costs little, between extremes it costs a lot. It is the κ reported by HelpSteer2.

hh-rlhf.d: Anthropic's preference dataset (Bai et al. 2022) on helpfulness and harmlessness, with full dialogues in chosen/rejected: 169,352 rows according to the card, MIT license.

ultrafeedback.d: An AI-labeled preference dataset: GPT-4 gave 1–5 scores on four aspects to 4 responses for each of 63,967 instructions. The binarized version has 61,135 training pairs (chosen = highest score).

helpsteer.d: NVIDIA datasets with human 0–4 Likert scores on five attributes (helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, verbosity); HelpSteer2-Preference and HelpSteer3 add −3…+3 preferences with justifications. CC-BY-4.0 license.

distribuicao-gumbel.d: An extreme-value distribution; you sample it with \(-\log(-\log U)\), \(U\) uniform. The difference of two independent Gumbels is logistic, which is why utilities with Gumbel noise produce exactly the Bradley–Terry sigmoid (and the Plackett–Luce softmax).

modelo-thurstone.d: The version of Bradley–Terry with normal noise (1927): \(P(i\succ j) = \Phi\big((r_i-r_j)/(\sqrt2\,s)\big)\). Nearly identical to the logistic with the same variance; it loses in practice because its gradient is less convenient.

elo.d: The chess rating, \(P(A\succ B) = 1/(1+10^{-(R_A-R_B)/400})\): it is Bradley–Terry in another base, with \(\Delta r = (\ln 10/400)\,\Delta R\). +400 Elo is equivalent to a 90.91% win rate.

plackett-luce.d: The generalization of Bradley–Terry to rankings of \(K\) items: 1st place comes from a softmax over all of them, 2nd place from a softmax over the remaining ones, and so on. With \(K=2\), it becomes BT.

normalizacao-do-rm.d: Adjusting the bias (and sometimes the scale) of the RM head, because the BT loss only sees differences: the zero is arbitrary. InstructGPT and Stiennon set the mean of the demonstrations/references to 0; Ziegler normalizes to mean 0 and variance 1.

margem-de-preferencia.d: Llama 2's variant of the RM loss: \(-\log\sigma(r_c - r_r - m)\), with a larger \(m\) for pairs marked as “much better” (up to 3 in the large version). It demands more separation on those pairs.

cabeca-escalar.d: A linear projection \(r = w^\top h + b\) that replaces the lm_head in an RM: it turns the final hidden state (read at the EOS token) into a single number. A multi-attribute RM uses several (5 in HelpSteer2).

calibracao-do-rm.d: A Bradley–Terry RM is calibrated when, among the pairs where it predicts \(\sigma(\Delta) = p\), humans agree in a fraction \(p\). It matters because, in RL, score differences become reward.

ece.d: \(\sum_b (n_b/N)\,|\text{acc}_b - \text{conf}_b|\): the weighted average, per confidence bin, of the distance between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Zero for a perfectly calibrated model.

escalonamento-por-temperatura.d: A recalibration that replaces \(\sigma(\Delta)\) with \(\sigma(\Delta/T)\) and fits only \(T\) to minimize the cross-entropy on a validation set. It does not change the order of the scores, so it does not alter best-of-\(n\).

rewardbench.d: An RM benchmark (Lambert et al. 2024): 2,985 prompt–chosen–rejected triples across Chat, Chat Hard, Safety, and Reasoning; the metric is pairwise accuracy. RewardBench 2 (2025) uses a best-of-4 format across 6 domains.

lei-de-goodhart.d: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” In RLHF: optimizing a proxy RM too hard exploits its errors. Relevant types: regressional (optimizing selects noise) and extremal (off-distribution, proxy and truth come apart).

superotimizacao.d: The regime in which the proxy RM score keeps rising while real quality (the “gold” score) falls. Gao et al. 2022 measured curves \(d(\alpha-\beta d)\) (best-of-\(n\)) and \(d(\alpha-\beta\log d)\) (RL), with \(d = \sqrt{\text{KL}}\).

vies-de-comprimento.d: The tendency of RMs (and judges) to prefer longer responses because of the “longer = better” correlation in the data. Singhal et al. 2023: 70–90% of PPO's reward gain on WebGPT and RLCD came from length.

best-of-n.d: Sampling \(n\) responses from the policy and keeping the one with the highest reward. It is optimization without training; the KL relative to the original policy is at most \(\log n - (n-1)/n\) nats (an upper bound, Beirami et al. 2024; nearly exact with distinct responses and no ties).

warm.d: Ramé et al. 2024: instead of averaging the predictions of several RMs, average the weights of RMs fine-tuned from the same pre-training. It costs a single RM at inference and holds up better under distribution shift.

orm.d: Outcome RM: the label for each step of a solution is whether the final answer is correct. It learns something like a value function (the chance of reaching the right answer).

prm.d: Process RM: predicts, after each step, whether the steps so far are correct. The solution's score is usually the product of the step probabilities. Good for reranking solutions; fragile as an RL reward at scale.

prm800k.d: An OpenAI dataset (Lightman et al. 2023) with 800 thousand human step labels (positive/negative/neutral) on 75 thousand solutions to 12 thousand MATH problems.

math-shepherd.d: Process labels without humans (Wang et al. 2023): from each step, a completer finishes \(N\) solutions; HE = 1 if any of them is right, SE = the fraction that is right (a Monte Carlo estimate of the step's value).

llm-como-juiz.d: Using a strong LLM to compare or score responses. GPT-4 agreed with humans 85% of the time on MT-bench (humans among themselves: 81%), but it has position, verbosity, and self-preference biases.

vies-de-posicao.d: The tendency of a judge (human or LLM) to favor the response that appears first (or second). It is mitigated by judging in both orders and averaging, or by counting a tie when the verdict flips with the order.

rm-generativo.d: A reward model that generates text: the score comes from the probability of a token (“Yes”) or from a critique written before the score, sometimes with voting across several critiques. More robust, but more expensive, because it requires decoding.
